title: India's Deadly Heat Is No Longer a Summer Problem. A New Study Says the Monsoon Is Next.
excerpt: Researchers from IIT Gandhinagar and Stanford found that uncompensable heat stress will engulf half the country during monsoon season under 2 degrees of warming. Up to 1.2 billion people are in the crosshairs.
body:
For decades, India's monsoon was the relief valve. The rains arrived, the mercury dropped, and the annual negotiation with lethal heat ended for another year.

That contract is being rewritten.

A study published this week in *AGU Advances*, authored by researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Gandhinagar, Stanford University, and Purdue University, found that **uncompensable heat stress** — the condition in which the human body physically cannot cool itself through sweating — is no longer confined to the summer months of March through June. It is surging into the monsoon season, and under 2 degrees Celsius of global warming, it could affect **53 per cent of India's landmass** between July and October.

The total population exposed could reach between 0.8 billion and 1.2 billion people.

## When Sweating Stops Working

Uncompensable heat stress is not the same as feeling hot. It occurs when the combination of air temperature and humidity overwhelms the body's evaporative cooling mechanism. Sustained exposure can cause organ failure and death, and no amount of hydration or shade can fully compensate for it.

The study analysed climate data from 1979 to 2021 and found that the geographic footprint of this condition has already expanded dramatically — from less than 0.01 million square kilometres in the 1980s to 0.04 million square kilometres by 2020. During summer, it now affects roughly eight per cent of India's land area.

But the monsoon numbers are what alarmed researchers. Historically, only one per cent of the country experienced uncompensable heat stress during the July-October window. Under projected warming, that figure could converge with summer levels.

"The monsoon season UHS, predominantly characterised by hot-humid conditions, is projected to increase rapidly with climate warming and affect nearly equivalent areas of the country as the summer season," the authors wrote.

## The Geography of Danger

The patterns are not uniform. Summer heat stress is concentrated in the Indo-Gangetic plain and along India's eastern coastline, driven by high temperatures and pre-monsoon moisture from the Bay of Bengal.

Monsoon heat stress operates differently. It emerges at a narrower air temperature range — between 35 and 38 degrees Celsius — but is made lethal by the crushing humidity that accompanies monsoonal moisture. Punjab, in northwestern India, has already experienced monsoon-season episodes.

The Gangetic Plain, northwestern India, and eastern coastal regions were identified as year-round hotspots. Under continued warming, the researchers found, "northwestern and Gangetic plain regions will face more frequent occurrences of UHS during the monsoon than in summer."

## A Cardiovascular Time Bomb

The health implications extend beyond heatstroke. A separate study published last month in *JAMA Cardiology* projected that the cardiovascular disease burden attributable to heat in the United States could nearly **triple by 2050** under high-emission scenarios — driven primarily by years of life lost rather than years lived with disability. Population aging alone accounted for a 34 per cent increase, independent of temperature changes.

For South Asians, who already carry the world's highest age-adjusted cardiovascular disease burden, heat amplifies an existing vulnerability. Outdoor workers, agricultural labourers, and the urban poor — categories that encompass hundreds of millions in the subcontinent — face compounding risks.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs planning summer visits home, the implications are immediate. July and August, once considered safe travel windows after the worst of summer, may no longer offer reliable respite. The monsoon breaks — periods of reduced rainfall within the season — are precisely when humid heat stress spikes.

Parents and grandparents in India, particularly those in the Indo-Gangetic belt, face escalating risk. Many lack access to air conditioning, and cultural habits of outdoor socialising, walking, and temple visits persist regardless of conditions.

India's Heat Action Plans, which now cover more than 140 cities and districts across 23 states, were largely designed using historical climate baselines. A 2023 review found that 95 per cent of them lacked formal heat risk assessments. Newer plans in cities like Thane are beginning to incorporate climate projections, but the gap between policy and reality remains vast.

The monsoon was supposed to be the safe season. The data says otherwise. For a billion people, the window of survivable heat just got shorter.
